d3-case-assessment.brief: Lowmoor Borough Council is building a model that reads incoming adult social-care referrals and suggests an urgency level; any referral the model is unsure about goes straight to a senior social worker. The council has already adopted AI principles, set up an oversight board, formed a multidisciplinary project team, and written policies covering standards, workflows and acceptable risk levels. A systems integrator will build the model, a hosting company will run it, and it will learn from the council's own case records plus anonymised referral data shared by a neighbouring authority. As the council's AIGP, you are scoping the impact assessment that must be finished before training and testing start, and you need to be precise about what that assessment is for and what it is not.
d3-case-assessment.steps[0].why: Used as a management tool, the impact assessment is about what could go wrong: residents wrongly marked as low urgency, unequal treatment of particular groups, misuse of sensitive records. It is not a tally of benefits. IAPP's own guidance describes its purpose more widely, as helping an organisation understand the good and the bad a system may bring (FSG p.6/8, Q2), so the two framings are compatible at different levels; this step concerns what the assessment is built to control. An accountability register and a legal-exposure review are useful documents, but they are different instruments.
d3-case-assessment.steps[1].why: A DPIA is the closest ready-made template because both instruments examine risk arising from how data is used. Extending that method into the ethical, social and legal questions specific to AI is far easier than starting from scratch. Safety and security assessments each look through a single narrow lens, and an environmental assessment answers a question this document is not responsible for.
d3-case-assessment.steps[2].why: Impact assessments focus on risks to people, to the organisation and to legal compliance: privacy, lawful data sourcing and unfair outcomes. For a narrow system like this one, electricity use falls outside that required core, although it is a fair topic in wider sustainability discussions. The other three items are standard content whatever the system's scope.
d3-case-assessment.steps[3].why: Doing the impact assessment before training exposes discrimination risk while data sourcing, labelling and design can still change, which is the whole reason for doing it early. Extra data does not cure a badly framed problem, and an independent audit or a bias bounty can only detect problems in a model that already exists.

d3-case-drift-alarm.brief: It is 6:15pm on the Thursday before a bank holiday. Corrie Mutual's automated claims-approval model has been live for nine months and settles roughly 2,500 home and motor claims each day. A governance alert fires: recall has fallen steeply, and a drift test shows that incoming claim data no longer resembles the data the model was trained on. In the same alert feed, a slower signal has been building for weeks: a fairness check shows claimants from one ethnic group are approved 1.4% less often than others, below Corrie's 1.5% escalation threshold but rising. You are the governance lead on call, and every decision you make over the next hour and the next month will be on the record.
d3-case-drift-alarm.steps[0].why: While a degraded model is still deciding real claims, the first priority is to stop further damage: remove it from the live flow and fall back to human handling before anything else. Diagnosis matters, but not while the model keeps making decisions; retraining automatically on the same shifted data may entrench the fault; and a customer notice issued before containment and investigation gets the order wrong.
d3-case-drift-alarm.steps[1].why: Incident response puts containment first because Corrie's model is still harming claimants with every decision it makes: stop the damage, then diagnose it. Investigation is necessary but comes second. Leading with customer messaging, or assuming a rollback is always the answer without first halting the live harm, skips the step that actually protects people right now.
d3-case-drift-alarm.steps[2].why: An escalation threshold sets a trigger for routine monitoring; it does not cap judgement. Where a protected group is affected, governance should escalate even when the figure sits under the line, because that is the defensible position if a regulator later asks why a known disparity was left alone. Waiting for the number to reach 1.5%, waiting for a scheduled meeting, or handling it quietly all treat the threshold as permission to delay, which is the exposure the rule exists to remove.
d3-case-drift-alarm.steps[3].why: Formal logging is the immediate step that sets everything else in motion: investigation, stakeholder notification, and corrective and preventive action (CAPA). A blameless review that still assigns owners for fixes is how findings become lasting process change rather than a one-off repair. Going straight to retraining, or closing tickets because the dashboards look normal, leaves no auditable record, and delaying stakeholder notice until CAPA is finished reverses an order governance relies on (SG).

d3-case-precode.brief: Kestrel Staffing places warehouse and logistics workers across three regions and wants software that ranks incoming applications so recruiters see the strongest candidates first. The managing director came back from a trade show convinced the agency is falling behind, and has promised the board a pilot within ninety days. You have been hired as AI governance lead before anything is built. A contractor has already pitched a deep-learning ranking engine in a slide deck, and an analyst has started copying ten years of old placement records into a spreadsheet to use as training data. This week your task is to put planning back in sequence: purpose, context, governance approach and the people affected first, technical build decisions later, and no money committed to the contractor's design until then.
d3-case-precode.steps[0].why: Planning starts by justifying the project: what outcome Kestrel wants, what it will cost, what it will gain, and whether a non-AI approach would do the job just as well. Testing and validation, impact assessment and appeal routes are all legitimate governance work, but each presupposes a defined system and a decision to go ahead. Doing them before the project has a justified purpose puts the lifecycle in the wrong order.
d3-case-precode.steps[1].why: An analysis that stops at internal efficiency ignores the people the system acts on. For a candidate-ranking tool the central question is who gets pushed down the list, and whether that is fair and lawful; it belongs in the analysis next to the savings. The other three options only stretch the same inward-looking financial view the managing director started with.
d3-case-precode.steps[2].why: Planning fixes the objective, assumptions, operating context and governance approach; it does not choose a model architecture. Whether the ranking engine ends up as a neural network, a gradient-boosted model or a simple scoring rule is decided in design and development, after planning has said what the system must achieve. The governance committee sets guardrails rather than picking techniques, and a hosting provider has no say in the choice.
d3-case-precode.steps[3].why: Stakeholder mapping is meant to steer risk assessment toward the people who live with the system's outputs. At Kestrel those are the applicants: an unfairly low ranking can cost someone a job, and none of the internal groups bears that consequence. Technical, compliance and leadership views all belong in the process, but they are inputs, not the people most exposed.
d3-case-precode.steps[4].why: Choosing an algorithm type is a technical judgement for the people who understand the data, the business context and the performance requirements, which here means Kestrel's own analytics team. The governance committee defines the risk limits the chosen approach must respect but does not select techniques. Note the difference from step 3: that step was about when architecture is decided, while this one is about who decides. A hosting provider or contractor can advise, but the authority stays inside Kestrel.

d3-case-release.brief: Fernhill Energy, a household gas and electricity supplier, plans to launch "Juno" next month: an in-house large language model that explains bills, sets up payment plans and passes complicated calls to human agents. The legal team fears liability for wrong advice about debt; the communications team fears headlines if Juno mistreats vulnerable customers. Before go-live you must decide whether Juno is genuinely ready, using the evidence from its shadow run, choosing the right document for each audience, and separating what customers are told from what stays inside Fernhill.
d3-case-release.steps[0].why: Shadow running with recorded outcomes counts as release-readiness evidence because the model meets real traffic and real edge cases without any customer bearing the cost of a mistake, much like running a new system in parallel before cutover. Claims of strong performance mean nothing to an auditor without recorded results; handing testing to an outsider with no internal review gives away governance's own responsibility; and a press announcement is marketing, not evidence (SG).
d3-case-release.steps[1].why: Intended use and known limitations mark out where Juno can responsibly be used. Deploying a model beyond that boundary is a frequent source of governance failure and legal exposure, which is precisely the lawyers' concern. Evaluation figures and training-data details belong in the same card but offer little protection if the model is used outside its tested scope, and energy use is a sustainability matter rather than the main readiness risk here.
d3-case-release.steps[2].why: The two documents are scoped differently by design. The model card is tied to a specific version and explains what that model is and how it should be used. The system dossier explains how the model sits within the live system, including the monitoring and conformity evidence the card does not repeat. Calling them duplicates, dividing them by public versus internal audience, or dividing them by data versus metrics all get the boundary wrong (SG).
d3-case-release.steps[3].why: Customers are owed an explanation of purpose, legal compliance and honest limitations, not Fernhill's trade secrets. Disclosure duties weigh public understanding against the organisation's legitimate interest in protecting its intellectual property, so purpose, compliance and limitations go in while the underlying techniques stay internal.
d3-case-release.steps[4].why: Retraining changes how the model reaches its outputs, so governance treats the result as a new release rather than a patch: full re-validation, refreshed documentation and transparency material, and formal approval before it serves customers again. This is separate from Case D's rule that containment comes first. Case D is about not retraining, or doing anything else, before a live incident is contained; this step says that whenever retraining happens, whether prompted by an incident or scheduled, the new version needs first-release rigour on its way back into service (SG).
